# Using R in this book {#sec-r .unnumbered}

Some chapters have short R exercises that run **in your browser**. You are not going to learn to program: you will use R as a powerful calculator to look inside some information tools. This chapter explains just what you need in ten minutes.

::: {.callout-note appearance="default"}
## Objectives
- Run and modify R code in the browser.
- Store values and text in objects and work with vectors.
:::

## How the code cells work

Each code block has a **Run Code** button. You can change the code and run it again; **Start Over** restores the original version. The first time you open a page, the browser downloads the R engine (a few seconds).

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
results <- 1250          # documents returned by a search
relevant <- 37           # the ones that are actually useful
relevant / results       # proportion
```

`<-` stores a value in an object. A **vector** groups several values with `c()`. Text goes in quotation marks:

```{webr}
sources <- c("Dialnet", "Google Scholar", "Scopus", "Wikipedia")
length(sources)                  # how many there are
"Scopus" %in% sources            # is Scopus there?
toupper(sources)                 # in capitals
```

### Exercise 1 {.unnumbered}

A search returns 480 results and, after reviewing them, 24 are relevant. Calculate the proportion of relevant results (the **precision** of the search).

```{webr}
#| exercise: r_precision
relevant <- 24
results <- ______
relevant / results
```

::: {.hint exercise="r_precision"}
Replace the blank with the total number of results.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="r_precision"}
```r
relevant <- 24
results <- 480
relevant / results
```
0.05: only one result in twenty is useful. In the chapter on retrieval you will see how to improve precision.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: r_precision
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.05))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 24 / 480 = 0.05.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Divide 24 by the total number of results (480).")
}
```

### Exercise 2 {.unnumbered}

Check whether "Dialnet" is in the vector `sources`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: r_in
#| setup: true
sources <- c("Dialnet", "Google Scholar", "Scopus", "Wikipedia")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: r_in
"______" %in% sources
```

::: {.hint exercise="r_in"}
Write the name exactly as it appears, with a capital first letter.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="r_in"}
```r
"Dialnet" %in% sources
```
`TRUE`. If you write "dialnet" in lower case, R says `FALSE`: it is case-sensitive, like some search engines.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: r_in
#| check: true
if (identical(.result, TRUE)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: Dialnet is in the vector.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Write \"Dialnet\" with a capital D.")
}
```

## Self-assessment

Answer all the questions and press **Show answers**: correct answers turn green, wrong ones red, and you will see your score. You can change your answers and check again. It does not count towards your mark.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
1. In R, text is written in quotation marks. {{< torf true >}}
2. To create a vector with several values you use the function {{< mcq "length()" "*c()" "toupper()" >}}
3. `length(c("a", "b", "c"))` returns {{< fitb "3" >}}
4. To do the exercises in this book you need to install R on your computer. {{< torf false >}}
:::

::: {.webex-solution boton="See explanations"}
- Without quotation marks, R would look for an object with that name.
- `c()` combines values into a vector.
- Three elements.
- They run in the browser with webR.
:::
